content: Acute high altitude illness encompasses a range of cerebral and pulmonary syndromes that can occur during travel to high altitudes, typically above 2500 meters, though it may also manifest at lower elevations in susceptible individuals. This condition includes acute mountain sickness (AMS), high altitude cerebral edema (HACE), and high altitude pulmonary edema (HAPE). Various pharmacological and non-pharmacological interventions are available for treatment, but their efficacy and safety remain uncertain. The objective of the study was to evaluate the clinical effectiveness and safety of these interventions, whether used alone or in combination, for treating acute high altitude illness. A systematic search was conducted across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and others, without language restrictions, to identify relevant randomized controlled trials (RCTs). The search was last updated on August 10, 2017. The review included 13 studies with a total of 468 participants, all of whom were adults, with two studies also including teenagers. Twelve studies focused on participants with AMS, while one study addressed HAPE. The studies were conducted in high-altitude regions, primarily in the European Alps, and follow-up periods were generally less than one day. The quality of evidence was frequently downgraded due to risks of bias and imprecision. Non-Pharmacological Interventions: Three studies involving 124 participants evaluated non-pharmacological interventions. None of these trials reported all-cause mortality or complete relief of AMS symptoms. One study with 64 participants found that a simulated descent of 193 millibars compared to 20 millibars might reduce AMS symptom severity after 12 hours of treatment, with an average reduction of 0.6 points on a clinical scale ranging from 0 to 11 (low-quality evidence). Another study with 29 participants found no complications associated with the use of hyperbaric chambers compared to supplementary oxygen (low-quality evidence). Pharmacological Interventions: Eleven trials involving 375 participants assessed pharmacological treatments. None of these trials reported all-cause mortality. One trial with 35 participants found that dexamethasone led to a higher proportion of participants achieving complete relief of AMS symptoms after 12 and 16 hours compared to placebo (47.1% vs. 0%, respectively; low-quality evidence). Another trial found that dexamethasone reduced AMS symptom severity, with a reported difference of 3.7 units on the AMS score (moderate-quality evidence). The effects of acetazolamide on symptom severity were uncertain when compared to placebo (standardized mean difference (SMD) −1.15, 95% CI −2.56 to 0.27; two studies, 25 participants; low-quality evidence). Similarly, the effects of gabapentin and magnesium on symptom severity were unclear. For gabapentin versus placebo, the mean visual analogue scale (VAS) scores were 2.92 versus 4.75, respectively (24 participants; low-quality evidence). For magnesium versus placebo, the mean scores were 9 and 10.3 units, respectively (25 participants; low-quality evidence). No adverse events were reported for either treatment (low-quality evidence). However, one trial comparing magnesium sulfate to placebo found that flushing was a common side effect in the magnesium sulfate group (75% vs. 7.7%, respectively; one study; 25 participants; low-quality evidence). Authors' Conclusions: The available evidence is limited and of low quality, making it difficult to draw definitive conclusions about the effectiveness and safety of non-pharmacological and pharmacological interventions for treating acute high altitude illness. Low-quality evidence suggests that dexamethasone and acetazolamide may reduce AMS scores compared to placebo, but the clinical benefits and potential harms of these treatments remain unclear. Overall, the findings have limited practical significance in clinical practice. High-quality research is urgently needed, as most of the included trials were poorly conducted and inadequately reported.
